Can you use toList() with forEach() in Java Streams?
questions.answer:
No. You cannot chain `toList()` with `forEach()` because `toList()` is a terminal operation that returns a `List<T>` and `forEach()` is also a terminal operation that returns void. You can only have one terminal operation per stream, and the stream is consumed once a terminal operation is called.

Wrong approach:

```java
// This will NOT compile
list.stream()
    .filter(x -> x > 5)
    .toList()           // Terminal operation - returns List
    .forEach(System.out::println); // Cannot chain after terminal operation
```

Option 1: use forEach() directly on the stream:

```java
list.stream()
    .filter(x -> x > 5)
    .forEach(System.out::println);
```

Option 2: collect to a list first, then iterate:

```java
List<Integer> filteredList = list.stream()
    .filter(x -> x > 5)
    .toList();

filteredList.forEach(System.out::println);
```

Option 3: use peek() for side effects while still collecting:

```java
List<Integer> result = list.stream()
    .filter(x -> x > 5)
    .peek(System.out::println) // Intermediate operation
    .toList();
```

Terminal operations: `forEach()`, `toList()`, `collect()`, `reduce()`, `count()`, `anyMatch()`. Intermediate operations: `filter()`, `map()`, `peek()`, `sorted()`, `distinct()`.

questions.question: What is the difference between GROUP BY and HAVING?
questions.answer:
`GROUP BY` groups rows that have the same values in the specified columns and is applied before aggregation, creating the groups that aggregate functions operate on. `HAVING` filters those groups after aggregation and can use aggregate functions in its condition. `WHERE` filters rows before grouping.

```sql
SELECT department, COUNT(*), AVG(salary)
FROM employees
WHERE hire_date > '2020-01-01'  -- Filter before grouping
GROUP BY department
HAVING COUNT(*) > 5;            -- Filter after grouping
```

questions.question: Explain Hexagonal Architecture and how you've implemented it.
questions.answer:
Hexagonal Architecture, also known as Ports and Adapters, isolates core business logic from external concerns, makes the application technology-agnostic, enables easy testing through mock adapters, and promotes loose coupling.

The hexagon (application core) contains business logic and domain models, is independent of external technologies, and defines the interfaces (ports) for external interaction.

Ports are interfaces that define how the core communicates with the outside world. Primary (driving/inbound) ports are triggered by external actors such as REST controllers or a CLI. Secondary (driven/outbound) ports are called by the core, such as repositories or message queues.

Adapters implement ports and handle the external technology details. Primary adapters are REST controllers, web interfaces and CLIs; secondary adapters are database implementations and external API clients.

A typical package structure:

```
com.example.user
├── domain/
│   ├── User.java
│   ├── UserDomainService.java
│   └── UserStatus.java
├── ports/
│   ├── inbound/
│   │   ├── UserUseCase.java
│   │   └── CreateUserCommand.java
│   └── outbound/
│       └── UserRepository.java
├── adapters/
│   ├── inbound/
│   │   ├── rest/
│   │   │   ├── UserRestAdapter.java
│   │   │   └── UserDto.java
│   │   └── cli/
│   │       └── UserCliAdapter.java
│   └── outbound/
│       ├── jpa/
│       │   ├── JpaUserRepositoryAdapter.java
│       │   └── UserEntity.java
│       └── memory/
│           └── InMemoryUserRepositoryAdapter.java
└── application/
    └── UserUseCaseImpl.java
```

Use it for complex domain logic that needs protection from external change, when multiple interfaces (REST, CLI, messaging) serve the same functionality, when testability requirements are high, for technology migration scenarios, and in domain-driven design implementations.

questions.question: What is Big O notation?
answer: Big O notation describes the worst-case time complexity of an algorithm as input size grows
O(1) constant time: HashMap get/put operations
O(log n) logarithmic: binary search, balanced tree operations
O(n) linear: array traversal, linear search
O(n log n) linearithmic: merge sort, heap sort
O(n squared) quadratic: nested loops, bubble sort
O(2^n) exponential: naive recursive Fibonacci
It describes growth rate rather than absolute time, ignores constants and lower-order terms, and focuses on the dominant factor as n approaches infinity

questions.question: How does GitFlow work?
questions.answer:
GitFlow is a branching model with specific branch types.

Main branches: `main`/`master` holds production-ready code, `develop` is the integration branch for features.

Supporting branches: `feature/*` for new features (branch from develop, merge back to develop), `release/*` to prepare releases (branch from develop, merge to main and develop), `hotfix/*` for critical production fixes (branch from main, merge to main and develop).

Workflow: create a feature branch from develop, work on the feature and merge it back to develop, create a release branch when ready, test the release and fix bugs then merge to main and develop, tag main with the version number, and for critical fixes create a hotfix branch from main.

questions.question: How do you restrict access to the backend pods so that only frontend pods can reach them?
questions.answer:
Use a NetworkPolicy.

```yaml
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: access
spec:
  podSelector:
    matchLabels:
      app: backend
  ingress:
  - from:
    - podSelector:
        matchLabels:
          app: frontend
```

questions.question: What is a necessary step to configure PurgeCSS in an Angular project?
